Online Income Tax Calculator: Old vs. New Tax Regime (FY 2025-26)

Navigating the nuances of Indian income tax computations can often feel overwhelming, particularly when deciding which tax structure suits your financial situation. The Online Income Tax Calculator (FY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27) is built to instantly compute your estimated tax liability, compare your outcomes across both tax regimes, and clarify how your salary breakdown, allowances, and investments impact your final tax payable.

How to Use the Indian Income Tax Calculator

To get the most accurate estimate from the calculator, gather your financial documents and follow these steps:

  1. Select Your Financial Year: Ensure the calculator is set to FY 2025-26 (Assessment Year 2026-27) to apply the correct active slab rates.

  2. Enter Gross Income Details: Input your salary components, including basic salary, dearness allowance, special allowances, and any income from other sources (such as interest or rental income).

  3. Input Allowances & Deductions (Old Regime): If you are evaluating the old tax regime, enter your actual rent paid for HRA calculations, life insurance premiums, PPF investments under Section 80C, health insurance under Section 80D, and home loan interest.

  4. Run the Comparison: Click calculate to view a side-by-side output showing your taxable income and net tax liability under both the Old and New Tax Regimes.

Calculator Methodology & Formula Logic

Understanding the underlying computational steps ensures you can audit your figures and verify how the tool derives your final tax payable.

Step 1: Gross Total Income & Allowances

The calculation begins by aggregating all streams of income into your Gross Total Income (GTI). From this aggregate figure, standard deductions (such as the standard salary deduction) and permissible exemptions like House Rent Allowance (HRA) or Leave Travel Allowance (LTA) under the old regime are subtracted to arrive at your net figure before Chapter VI-A deductions.

Step 2: Deductions & Exemptions (Old Regime)

Under the Old Tax Regime, eligible deductions such as investments under Section 80C (capped at ₹1,50,000), medical insurance under Section 80D, and interest paid on housing loans under Section 24 are subtracted from your taxable base. Under the New Tax Regime, these specific deductions are omitted in exchange for lower baseline tax rates.

Step 3: Tax Slab Computation & Rebates (Section 87A)

Once net taxable income is determined, applicable slab rates are applied. After computing the tentative tax, the tool factors in the tax rebate under Section 87A and any applicable marginal relief, followed by the addition of health and education cess (4%).

Income Tax Slabs & Rates for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)

Tax liability varies significantly depending on the regime you select. The tables below outline the active slabs for the current financial year.

(Note: Senior citizens and super senior citizens enjoy higher basic exemption thresholds of ₹3,00,000 and ₹5,00,000 respectively under the old regime).

Key Differences: Old Tax Regime vs. New Tax Regime

Choosing the right structure requires balancing deductions against tax rates:

  • Deductions: The Old Regime permits over 70 tax exemptions and deductions (including 80C, 80D, HRA, and LTA). The New Regime removes almost all deductions, though the standard deduction applies to salaried individuals under both structures.

  • Tax Slabs: The New Regime features wider tax slabs and lower baseline rates at various income tiers, making it beneficial for individuals with minimal traditional investments.

  • Flexibility: Salaried individuals can generally switch between regimes annually when filing their Income Tax Returns (ITR), whereas business owners face stricter limitations on switching.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

  • 1. Which tax regime should I choose using the calculator?

    If your total deductions (HRA, 80C, 80D, home loan interest) exceed the threshold where the lower tax rates of the New Regime become more advantageous, the Old Regime usually results in lower tax payable. Use the calculator to test your exact figures.

  • 2. Is the Standard Deduction available in both tax regimes?

    Yes, the standard deduction is available to salaried individuals and pensioners under both the Old and New Tax Regimes for FY 2025-26.

  • 3. What documents do I need before using the calculator?

    Keep your current salary slips, Form 16 (if available), rent receipts or agreements if claiming HRA, and investment proofs for Section 80C and 80D handy.

  • 4. How does the Section 87A rebate work?

    Section 87A provides a tax rebate that can eliminate tax liability entirely if your net taxable income falls below specified statutory limits under each regime.

  • 5. Can I switch my tax regime after submitting investment proofs to my employer?

    Yes. Even if you declare one regime to your employer for TDS deduction purposes, you have the legal right to choose the alternative regime when filing your personal ITR at the end of the financial year.

  • 6. Are maintenance charges included when calculating HRA exemptions?

    No. Only the core rent paid to the landlord is considered; separate utility bills and society maintenance fees are excluded.

  • 7. What happens if my income exceeds ₹50 lakhs?

    High-income earners are subject to a surcharge on their income tax liability. The calculator incorporates applicable surcharge tiers based on your gross income input.

  • 8. Does the calculator account for cess?

    Yes, the final computed tax output automatically adds the standard 4% Health and Education Cess mandated by the Income Tax Act.

  • 9. Is my financial data stored when I use this online tool?

    No calculations or financial figures input into the browser utility are retained on external servers, ensuring complete privacy.

  • 10. Can freelancers use this income tax calculator?

    While the tool accommodates standard salary breakdowns, freelancers and business owners should also account for professional expenses and presumptive taxation provisions under Section 44AD.

Important Legal & Verification Notices

This calculator and guide are provided for estimation, educational simulation, and tax planning purposes only. Tax laws are subject to amendment, and individual circumstances vary. Users are strongly advised to verify all computed tax liabilities and consult a qualified Chartered Accountant (CA) or review official CBDT portals prior to filing official Income Tax Returns (ITR).

faqs.question: Do I need to create an account to use an online tax calculator?
faqs.answer: No. Most quality online tax calculators allow you to run instant estimates anonymously without requiring registration or logins.

faqs.question: Are online tax calculations legally binding for filing?
faqs.answer: No. Calculators are estimation tools designed to help you plan. Your final tax liability is determined when you officially file your Income Tax Return (ITR) on the government portal.

faqs.question: Can freelancers and business owners use a standard tax calculator?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided the calculator includes fields for business income, professional receipts, and allowable business expenses alongside regular salary inputs.

faqs.question: What happens if I make a mistake while entering my deductions?
faqs.answer: Since the calculator is an estimation tool, any input error simply alters the estimated output. You can re-enter the correct figures instantly to see the revised tax amount.

faqs.question: Is capital gains tax calculated automatically by online calculators?
faqs.answer: It depends on the platform. Advanced calculators provide specific input fields for short-term and long-term capital gains so they can apply the correct separate tax rates.

faqs.question: How often are online tax calculators updated with new budget rules?
faqs.answer: Reliable tax calculator platforms update their backend logic immediately following the Union Budget announcements and official notifications issued for the relevant financial year.

faqs.question: What is marginal relief, and how does it save me money if my income slightly exceeds ₹12 Lakhs?
faqs.answer: If your taxable income crosses ₹12 Lakhs under the New Tax Regime, your tax liability cannot exceed the amount of income earned above ₹12 Lakhs. Marginal relief absorbs the difference so you don't lose more money in tax than you did in extra earnings.

faqs.question: Is the 4% Health and Education Cess added automatically by tax calculators?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reliable online calculators compute your base tax across slabs, apply any eligible Section 87A rebates, and then add a final 4% Health and Education Cess to arrive at your net payable tax.

faqs.question: Can I claim an employer's NPS contribution under the New Tax Regime?
faqs.answer: Yes. Employer contributions to the National Pension System under Section 80CCD(2)—up to 14% of your basic salary—are deductible even if you choose the New Tax Regime.

faqs.question: What is the maximum surcharge difference between the Old and New Tax Regimes for high earners?
faqs.answer: For ultra-high-income earners with taxable income exceeding ₹5 Crores, the peak surcharge rate under the Old Tax Regime is 37%, whereas the New Tax Regime caps the maximum surcharge at 25%.

faqs.question: What happens if I miss the July 31st ITR filing deadline after calculating my tax?
faqs.answer: If you miss the standard July 31 deadline for non-audit cases, you can still file a belated return until December 31st of the assessment year, though it attracts late fees under Section 234F and potential interest penalties.

faqs.question: How does the ₹75,000 standard deduction make a salary of up to ₹12,75,000 tax-free under the New Regime?
faqs.answer: When your gross salary is ₹12,75,000, subtracting the ₹75,000 standard deduction brings your net taxable income down exactly to ₹12,00,000. The resulting tax liability is then entirely offset by the Section 87A rebate, resulting in zero net tax.

faqs.question: What happens if my salary changes mid-year? Should I recalculate quarterly?

faqs.answer: No. Statutory contributions to recognized Employee Provident Funds (EPF) and tax-exempt limits on gratuity or leave encashment are governed by separate statutory provisions and remain unaffected by your choice of tax regime.

faqs.answer: Yes. Your declaration to your employer is only meant for calculating monthly TDS deductions. When filing your Income Tax Return (ITR) at the end of the year, you are completely free to choose whichever regime is more beneficial, provided you do not have business or professional income restrictions.

faqs.question: How does Section 194Q on purchase of goods work?
faqs.answer: Buyers with gross business turnover exceeding ₹10 Crores in the preceding financial year must deduct TDS @ 0.1% on purchase of goods from a resident seller if total purchases exceed ₹50,00,000 in the current FY. TDS is computed strictly on the value exceeding ₹50 Lakhs.

faqs.question: When is TDS under Section 194S applicable on Crypto and Virtual Digital Assets?
faqs.answer: TDS @ 1% is deducted by the buyer or crypto exchange on consideration paid for the transfer of Virtual Digital Assets (cryptocurrency, tokens, NFTs) if the annual transaction value exceeds ₹10,000 (or ₹50,000 for specified individual buyers with no business income).

faqs.question: What is the due date for depositing TDS and filing quarterly returns?
faqs.answer: TDS deducted during any calendar month must be deposited to the government treasury by the 7th day of the subsequent month (April 30th for March). Quarterly returns (Form 24Q for salary, Form 26Q for non-salary) are due by July 31 (Q1), October 31 (Q2), January 31 (Q3), and May 31 (Q4).

faqs.question: How does the payee get credit for the TDS deducted?
faqs.answer: Once the deductor files the quarterly TDS return, the tax credit is mapped to the payee's PAN and reflected in their Annual Information Statement (AIS) and Form 26AS. The deductor also issues Form 16A (for non-salary) or Form 16 (for salary) generated from the TRACES portal.

author.bio: Practicing Chartered Accountant specializing in direct taxation.

posts.content:
Executive Summary Essential Financial Literacy Guide

Don't Get Fooled by "Headline Interest Rates": APR Reveals the True Cost of Your Loan

When comparing loan offers from banks and NBFCs, picking the lowest stated interest rate can cost you tens of thousands of rupees in hidden processing fees, documentation charges, and insurance premiums. Annual Percentage Rate (APR) combines interest plus all upfront fees into one annual percentage, giving you the only true apple-to-apples metric to identify the cheapest loan.

Interest Rate
Cost of Principal

Excludes fees & processing costs

APR Metric
True Annual Cost

Interest + Fees + Mandates

RBI Mandate
Key Facts Statement

Mandatory disclosure for all loans

Interest Rate vs. APR: Understanding the Fundamental Difference

When you apply for a personal loan, home loan, or car loan, lenders showcase advertised interest rates on billboards and ads. However, what you actually pay out of pocket involves additional fees that increase your total borrowing burden.

Headline Metric Basic Rate

Stated Interest Rate

The percentage fee charged by the lender purely on the borrowed principal amount over a year.

Used to compute monthly Equated Monthly Instalments (EMIs)
Ignores processing fees & stamp duty
Ignores insurance & verification charges
True Cost Metric Recommended

Annual Percentage Rate (APR)

The comprehensive annual cost of credit expressed as a percentage, factoring interest plus all mandatory upfront charges.

Includes processing fees, GST, documentation & insurance
Calculated on net cash disbursed into your bank account
Mandated by RBI in Key Facts Statement (KFS)

Real-World Example: Why Loan B Wins Despite a Higher Interest Rate

Consider a loan scenario where you need a ₹5,00,000 personal loan for 3 years (36 months). You receive offers from two competing lenders:

Case Study

₹5,00,000 Personal Loan Comparison (3-Year Tenure)

Net Disbursement Cost
Loan Parameter Lender A (High Fee) Lender B (Low Fee)
Loan Principal Amount ₹5,00,000 ₹5,00,000
Advertised Interest Rate 11.5% p.a. (Lower) 12.0% p.a. (Higher)
Upfront Processing Fee + GST ₹15,000 (3% + GST) ₹3,500 (Flat Fee)
Net Money Disbursed to Bank ₹4,85,000 ₹4,96,500
Monthly EMI (36 Months) ₹16,482 ₹16,607
Total Outflow (Fee + 36 EMIs) ₹6,08,352 ₹6,01,352
Effective APR (True Annual Cost) 13.84% APR 12.52% APR Winner: Saves ₹7,000!
!
Key Takeaway: Even though Lender A advertised a lower 11.5% interest rate, its heavy ₹15,000 processing fee raised its true annual cost (APR) to 13.84%. Lender B is ₹7,000 cheaper overall despite having a higher headline interest rate!

What Fees Are Covered in APR Calculations?

Under financial standards and central banking guidelines, APR accounts for all mandatory recurring and non-recurring costs required to obtain the loan:

1

Processing & Admin Fees

Upfront charges deducted during loan disbursement.

2

Documentation & Stamps

Legal agreement, e-stamping, and verification fees.

3

Credit Life Insurance

Compulsory loan protection insurance bundled by lender.

RBI Key Facts Statement (KFS) Rule for Indian Borrowers

To protect retail borrowers from misleading financial advertisements, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) made it compulsory for all regulated entities (banks, NBFCs, and digital lending apps) to issue a standardized Key Facts Statement (KFS) before executing any loan contract.

RBI Regulatory Mandate Consumer Protection Framework

What Lenders Must Disclose in Your Key Facts Statement (KFS):

  • Exact Annual Percentage Rate (APR)
  • Itemized breakdown of all upfront fees
  • Net disbursed amount vs gross sanction amount
  • Complete EMI repayment schedule table
  • Prepayment penalty terms & foreclosure clauses
  • Nodal Grievance Officer details

4-Step Checklist to Compare Loan Offers Like a Pro

1

Request the Key Facts Statement (KFS) First

Never accept an offer verbally or based on marketing flyers. Demand the official KFS document from the bank officer.

2

Compare APR with APR (Apple-to-Apples)

Only compare APRs across loans with identical tenure and similar borrowing amounts for accurate results.

3

Check Net In-Hand Disbursement

Calculate: Net Disbursed Amount = Sanctioned Principal - (Processing Fee + GST + Insurance).

4

Review Foreclosure & Part-Payment Penalties

Under RBI norms, floating rate personal loans to individuals carry 0% foreclosure fees, but fixed rate loans may attract 2% to 5% charges.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why is APR higher than the advertised interest rate?

APR includes both the annual interest charge AND all mandatory upfront fees (processing fees, documentation, GST, insurance) distributed across the loan tenure, making it higher than the nominal interest rate.

Q: Can APR and interest rate ever be equal?

Yes! If a lender waives 100% of processing fees, documentation charges, and insurance costs, the APR will exactly equal the interest rate.

Q: Is KFS mandatory for all Indian loans?

Yes, per RBI guidelines, all regulated banks, NBFCs, and fintech platforms must provide a standardized Key Facts Statement (KFS) before loan execution.

author.bio: Practicing Chartered Accountant specializing in direct taxation.
author.name: CA Rajesh Sharma

posts.seoTitle: Hidden Loan Costs: How Fees & Insurance Impact Your Borrowing Cost
posts.content:
A loan with a low interest rate can still turn out to be expensive.

That sounds surprising at first, especially when most loan advertisements put the interest rate in the biggest font. But the rate is only one part of what you pay. Processing fees, insurance, legal and valuation charges, documentation costs, taxes on applicable services and other fees can add to the final bill.

The easiest way to avoid confusion is to stop looking at the interest rate on its own.

Instead, ask a more practical question: How much money will I actually receive, and how much will I have to pay back by the time the loan is finished?

That gives you a much better picture of what the borrowing is really costing you.

What Is the Effective Cost of Borrowing?

The effective cost of borrowing is the overall cost you bear for getting and using a loan. It can include the interest charged on the loan as well as applicable processing fees, insurance premiums, legal or valuation expenses, taxes and other mandatory charges.

The exact cost depends on the type of loan, lender, loan amount, tenure and the terms offered to you.

For applicable loans, the RBI's Key Facts Statement framework is intended to make important loan terms and the overall cost easier for borrowers to understand and compare. The KFS includes information such as the APR and repayment schedule.

This is useful because the number advertised in a loan campaign isn't necessarily the number that tells you everything about the transaction.

Why the Interest Rate Alone Is Not Enough to Compare Loans

Suppose you need a ₹5 lakh loan and receive two offers.

One lender quotes 10.75% and another quotes 11%.

At first glance, the 10.75% offer looks cheaper. But now imagine the first lender charges ₹12,000 in applicable upfront costs while the second charges ₹4,000.

The difference in interest rate is only 0.25 percentage points. Whether that lower rate actually saves you more than the additional ₹8,000 depends on the loan amount, tenure and repayment schedule.

This is why comparing loans requires more than finding the smallest percentage.

You should look at the interest rate, EMI, total interest, fees, net amount received, total repayment and, where applicable, the APR shown in the lender's documents.

How Upfront Processing Fees and Deductions Affect Your Loan Disbursal

One of the most important numbers to check is the amount that actually reaches your bank account.

Suppose a lender sanctions a loan of ₹5,00,000 and deducts ₹8,000 in applicable upfront charges. Your sanctioned amount is still ₹5 lakh, but the amount you receive could be ₹4,92,000.

That difference matters if you borrowed the money for a specific purpose.

If you need ₹5 lakh to pay a supplier, purchase equipment or cover an important expense, receiving ₹4.92 lakh may leave you with a shortfall.

So before accepting a loan, ask the lender:

"What will be the exact net amount credited to my account after all deductions?"

The answer is often more useful than simply knowing the sanctioned amount.

How Much Can a Loan Processing Fee Add to Your Cost?

Processing fees are commonly charged as either a percentage of the loan amount, a flat amount, or a percentage subject to minimum or maximum limits.

Consider a simple 1% fee:

Loan amount

1% processing fee

₹2 lakh

₹2,000

₹5 lakh

₹5,000

₹10 lakh

₹10,000

₹25 lakh

₹25,000

₹50 lakh

₹50,000

The percentage stays the same, but the actual rupee cost rises quickly as the loan gets larger.

Actual lender policies vary. Some lenders have minimum fees, maximum caps or different charges for different loan products. Current lender disclosures illustrate that there is no single processing-fee structure that applies across every type of loan.

That is why you should always check the actual fee applicable to your loan rather than assuming that a percentage shown in a general article applies to you.

Flat Processing Fee vs Percentage-Based Fee: Which Costs Less?

The answer depends on the loan amount.

Imagine one lender charges a fixed ₹5,000 processing fee while another charges 1% of the loan amount.

For a ₹2 lakh loan:

  • Fixed fee = ₹5,000

  • 1% fee = ₹2,000

For a ₹10 lakh loan:

  • Fixed fee = ₹5,000

  • 1% fee = ₹10,000

The cheaper option changes because the percentage-based fee increases with the loan amount.

This is a good example of why percentages can sometimes be misleading when you're trying to understand your actual cost.

Whenever you see a percentage, convert it into rupees.

That is the number that comes out of your pocket.

How GST and Other Taxes Can Increase Loan-Related Charges

Some loan-related services and fees may attract applicable taxes.

The important word here is applicable. You shouldn't automatically add the same tax percentage to every charge you see on a loan document.

The lender's current fee schedule should tell you how a particular charge is treated.

For example, if a processing fee is quoted separately from applicable taxes, the amount you eventually pay can be higher than the headline processing fee.

A simple question can clear this up:

"Is this fee inclusive of applicable taxes, or will taxes be charged separately?"

Ask this before you compare one lender's fee with another.

How Insurance Can Increase the Overall Cost of a Loan

Insurance can sometimes be offered alongside a loan, particularly with secured lending.

The important thing is to understand exactly what the insurance covers and whether it is mandatory or optional for your particular loan.

For example, property insurance can arise in connection with a home loan or another loan secured against property. Some lenders also offer loan-protection or life-insurance products.

These are not necessarily the same thing.

Before accepting an insurance product, ask:

  • What does the policy cover?

  • Is it compulsory?

  • Who is providing the insurance?

  • What is the total premium?

  • Is the premium paid separately?

  • Is it deducted from the loan disbursal?

  • Is it being added to the amount financed?

  • What happens to the policy if the loan is closed early?

Current lender disclosures show that property insurance and other related costs can appear separately from the basic processing fee.

The key point is not to assume that every insurance product offered with a loan is compulsory.

Read the terms and ask.

What Happens If an Insurance Premium Is Added to the Loan?

This is where the cost can become less obvious.

Suppose you borrow ₹5 lakh and an insurance premium of ₹10,000 is added to the financed amount.

You aren't simply paying ₹10,000 for insurance anymore. If the premium becomes part of the amount on which interest is calculated, you could also pay interest on that financed premium.

The exact treatment depends on the loan structure and lender.

So if insurance is being financed, ask:

"Will interest also be charged on the insurance premium?"

That one question can tell you whether the insurance is simply an additional expense or whether it is also increasing the amount on which you pay interest.

What Are Legal, Valuation and Documentation Charges on Loans?

These charges are particularly relevant when you take a secured loan.

A home loan or Loan Against Property, for example, may require the lender to verify the property's legal ownership and assess its value.

Depending on the product and lender, you may therefore encounter costs related to:

  • Legal verification

  • Property valuation

  • Technical inspection

  • Document verification

  • Mortgage-related work

  • Registration or statutory requirements

  • Other applicable services

These expenses are not necessarily hidden. They may be listed in the lender's fee schedule or loan documents.

The problem is that borrowers sometimes focus so heavily on the processing fee that they forget to ask about everything else.

Current bank disclosures show that legal, valuation and other property-related charges can be listed separately or handled as part of a broader processing structure, depending on the lender.

Why Legal and Valuation Charges Matter More for Property Loans

With an unsecured personal loan, there usually isn't a property for the lender to inspect and value.

A property-backed loan is different.

The lender has to establish that the property can be accepted as security and determine its value under the lender's process.

That can introduce costs that a borrower taking a simple unsecured loan may never encounter.

For this reason, comparing two property loans only by their processing fees can give you the wrong impression.

One lender might advertise a higher processing fee but include certain services in it.

Another might advertise a lower processing fee and charge some services separately.

Always compare the combined applicable charges, not just the first fee you see.

Why the Amount You Receive Can Be More Important Than the Amount Sanctioned

Consider this situation.

A lender approves:

₹10,00,000

But applicable upfront costs total:

₹15,000

If those costs are deducted before disbursement, you could receive:

₹9,85,000

You may have applied for ₹10 lakh because you actually need ₹10 lakh.

In that case, the ₹15,000 deduction isn't just a minor accounting detail. It affects whether the loan gives you enough money to do what you planned.

This is particularly important for business loans, property-related expenses, medical costs, education expenses and other situations where you have a specific payment to make.

How Loan Fees Affect Short-Term Borrowing More Than Long-Term Borrowing

A fixed fee can have a noticeable impact when you borrow for a short period.

Imagine paying ₹10,000 in upfront charges for a loan that you plan to repay in six months.

The same ₹10,000 charge on a seven-year loan is still ₹10,000, but its effect on the overall economics of the borrowing is different.

This is one reason the tenure should always be considered alongside the fees.

A loan's cost isn't just about how much you pay. It's also about when you pay it.

Can a Lower EMI Loan Actually Cost More?

Yes.

This is one of the easiest traps to fall into when comparing loan offers.

Suppose one loan has an EMI of ₹18,000 for three years and another has an EMI of ₹14,000 for five years.

The second loan feels more comfortable because ₹14,000 is easier to fit into the monthly budget.

But you're making payments for two additional years.

The total interest can therefore be considerably higher.

Add processing fees, insurance and other applicable charges, and the cheaper-looking EMI may not represent the cheaper loan.

That's why you should look at the EMI and the total repayment together.

EMI tells you about monthly affordability.

Total repayment tells you about the overall cost.

You need both.

How to Calculate the Total Cost of a Loan

A simple starting point is to look at the total scheduled repayments and then account for applicable costs that are not already included.

For example:

Cost

Amount

Total EMI payments

₹5,80,000

Processing fee

₹7,500

₹1,500

Other applicable charges

₹1,000

Total broad cost

₹5,90,000

This gives you a practical first estimate.

For an official comparison, however, use the lender's repayment schedule, applicable APR and written fee disclosures rather than relying on a rough calculation.

How Financing a Fee Can Increase the Cost Further

There is a difference between paying a fee yourself and borrowing money to pay that fee.

Suppose your loan is ₹5 lakh and the lender adds a ₹10,000 charge to the financed amount.

The amount being financed is now higher.

If interest is charged on that additional amount, you're effectively paying interest on a fee.

This isn't automatically wrong or unusual, but it changes the economics of the loan.

Whenever a lender says a charge will be "added to the loan," ask what the new financed amount will be and whether interest will be calculated on it.

Are "Hidden Charges" Really Hidden?

Not always.

Many charges that borrowers later call "hidden" were actually mentioned somewhere in the paperwork.

They may have appeared in:

  • The fee schedule

  • Sanction letter

  • Key Facts Statement

  • Loan agreement

  • Disbursement statement

  • Product terms

The bigger problem is often that borrowers don't know which figures to look for.

That is why reading the documents matters.

If a charge is clearly disclosed before you agree to the loan, you can include it in your comparison.

If you don't understand a charge, ask the lender to explain it before signing.

How the RBI Key Facts Statement Helps Borrowers Compare Loan Costs

For applicable loans, the RBI's Key Facts Statement provides a standardised way of presenting important loan information.

The framework includes the Annual Percentage Rate and a repayment schedule, helping borrowers see the broader cost rather than relying only on the advertised interest rate.

The RBI's framework also provides for certain third-party charges recovered through the regulated entity, such as applicable insurance and legal charges, to be reflected in the APR and disclosed separately.

This is useful when comparing offers because the interest rate alone may not tell the full story.

When you receive a KFS, don't just look for the rate.

Look at the cost section and repayment schedule too.

APR vs Interest Rate: Why the Difference Matters

The interest rate is the rate used to calculate interest under the loan's terms.

APR is a broader annualised measure of the cost of credit under the applicable framework and can take relevant charges into account.

That makes APR useful when comparing similar loan offers.

Imagine two lenders both quote an 11% interest rate.

If one loan has significantly higher applicable charges, the overall annualised cost can be different.

So when an applicable KFS gives you an APR, don't ignore it.

It gives you another number to use alongside the interest rate.

But you should still understand the individual charges that make up the difference.

Why You Should Compare the Same Loan Amount and Tenure

Loan comparisons can become misleading if the basic assumptions are different.

For example, comparing:

₹5 lakh for 3 years

with:

₹5 lakh for 5 years

doesn't tell you much about which lender is cheaper unless you account for the different repayment periods.

Similarly, comparing ₹5 lakh from one lender with ₹10 lakh from another makes percentage-based charges harder to interpret.

For a clean comparison, start with the same:

  • Loan amount

  • Tenure

  • Repayment frequency

  • Borrower situation, where possible

Then compare the rate and charges.

You don't need a complicated spreadsheet.

What Borrowers Should Ask Before Signing a Loan

You don't need to sound like a financial expert when speaking to a lender.

A few straightforward questions are enough:

  1. How much has been sanctioned?

  2. How much will actually be credited to me?

  3. What is the interest rate?

  4. How is the interest calculated?

  5. What will my EMI be?

  6. How much interest will I pay over the full tenure?

  7. What is the processing fee?

  9. Is insurance mandatory or optional?

  10. Will any fee or insurance premium be added to the loan?

  11. What APR is shown in my KFS, where applicable?

  12. What happens if I prepay or close the loan early?

  13. What charges apply if an EMI is delayed or fails?

These questions are much more useful than simply asking:

"What is your lowest interest rate?"

A Simple Worked Comparison

Let's say you are considering two loans of ₹5 lakh for three years.

Loan A

  • Interest rate: 10.75%

  • Processing fee: ₹10,000

  • Other applicable charges: ₹2,000

  • Insurance: ₹8,000

Loan B

  • Interest rate: 11%

  • Processing fee: ₹4,000

  • Other applicable charges: ₹1,500

  • Insurance: ₹0

Loan A has the lower interest rate.

But it also has significantly higher upfront costs.

The difference in listed additional costs is:

Loan A: ₹20,000

Loan B: ₹5,500

That's a difference of:

₹14,500

Now the real question becomes:

Does the 0.25 percentage-point interest-rate advantage of Loan A save more than ₹14,500 over the three-year repayment period?

You need the actual EMI and repayment figures to answer that.

This is exactly why comparing the interest rate alone can be misleading.

Why the Cheapest Loan on Paper May Not Be the Best Fit for You

There is another side to this.

The lowest total cost isn't the only thing a borrower should consider.

You also need a loan that fits your circumstances.

For example, one lender may have a slightly higher cost but a repayment schedule that fits your cash flow better.

Another may offer a lower rate but require a loan structure that doesn't suit your needs.

A business owner with seasonal income may look at repayment flexibility differently from someone receiving a fixed monthly salary.

Someone planning to repay a loan early should pay more attention to the applicable prepayment terms.

So the comparison should be practical, not just mathematical.

What About Prepayment and Foreclosure Charges?

If you expect to close the loan early, check these terms before taking it.

A loan may look attractive when calculated over the full tenure, but your actual plan could be to repay it much earlier.

Check:

  • Whether part-prepayment is allowed

  • Minimum part-prepayment amount

  • Applicable foreclosure charges

  • Any lock-in period

  • Notice requirements

  • Other conditions

The rules can differ according to the type of loan and borrower.

Don't rely on a generic statement such as "there are no prepayment charges."

Read the terms that apply to your specific product.

What About Late Payment and Bounce Charges?

These aren't costs you should expect to pay if everything goes smoothly, but they're still worth knowing.

Loan documents may specify charges for:

  • Delayed EMI payments

  • Failed auto-debits

  • Payment or cheque bounces

  • Other default-related events

If you're already stretching your monthly budget to afford a loan, these terms become even more important.

A loan that looks manageable on paper can become much harder to handle if missed-payment charges start accumulating.

A Useful Rule: Separate "Cost" From "Convenience"

Sometimes borrowers focus so heavily on getting the lowest rate that they ignore the rest of the borrowing experience.

A loan may have a low rate but a complicated fee structure.

Another may cost slightly more but have terms that are easier for you to understand and manage.

This doesn't mean you should pay more simply for convenience.

It means the decision should be based on the complete offer.

You want to know exactly what you are signing up for.

The Three Numbers You Should Always Know

If you remember nothing else from this article, remember these three numbers:

1. Amount sanctioned

How much the lender is approving.

2. Amount actually received

How much money reaches your account after applicable deductions.

3. Total amount you are expected to repay

What the repayment schedule requires you to pay over the loan term.

Once you know these three figures, the rest of the loan becomes much easier to understand.

Final Takeaway: Look at the Whole Loan, Not Just the Rate

A low interest rate is useful.

It can reduce your interest cost.

But it doesn't automatically make a loan cheap.

Processing fees, insurance, legal and valuation expenses, documentation charges, taxes on applicable services and other costs can change the amount you actually spend.

The difference becomes particularly important when the loan is large, the tenure is short, or substantial upfront charges are deducted from the disbursement.

The safest approach is straightforward: find out how much you will actually receive, how much you will repay, and what charges sit between those two numbers.

For applicable loans, use the lender's Key Facts Statement and repayment schedule as your main reference. Look at the APR as well as the interest rate, and check every charge that applies to your specific offer.

Don't let a big "10.99%" or "8.50%" headline make the decision for you.

Read the smaller numbers too.

That's where the real cost of borrowing often becomes clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a loan with a lower interest rate cost more?

Yes. A lower rate can be offset by higher processing fees, insurance premiums or other applicable charges. The actual answer depends on the loan amount, tenure, repayment schedule and complete cost structure.

What is included in the cost of borrowing?

It can include interest and applicable processing, documentation, legal, valuation, insurance, tax and other mandatory charges. The exact list depends on the loan product and lender.

Does a processing fee reduce the loan amount?

It can reduce the amount you actually receive if the fee is deducted before disbursement. The sanctioned loan amount and net amount credited to your account can therefore be different.

Can I be charged interest on a processing fee?

If the fee is financed and added to the loan amount, the treatment may result in interest being charged on that additional amount. Check the lender's specific terms.

Is insurance compulsory with every loan?

No. Insurance requirements depend on the loan product and lender. Ask whether the specific insurance being offered is mandatory or optional.

Why are legal and valuation charges common in property loans?

The lender may need to verify the property's legal ownership and assess its value before accepting it as security. Those checks can create separate costs.

What is the difference between APR and the interest rate?

The interest rate is the rate used to calculate interest under the loan terms. APR is a broader annualised measure of borrowing cost under the applicable framework and can include relevant charges.

What is a Key Facts Statement?

A Key Facts Statement is a standardised loan document that provides important information about applicable loans, including key costs, APR and repayment details.

Should I compare processing fees separately?

Yes, but don't stop there. A lender with a lower processing fee may have other charges that make the overall loan more expensive.

Should I choose the loan with the lowest EMI?

Not automatically. A lower EMI can result from a longer tenure, which can increase total interest. Compare the EMI with total repayment and the complete borrowing cost.

What is the best way to compare two loan offers?

Use the same loan amount and tenure where possible, then compare the interest rate, EMI, total interest, net amount received, processing fee, insurance, other applicable charges, APR and prepayment terms.

posts.seoTitle: How to Calculate the True Cost of a Loan (Beyond Interest Rate)
posts.content:
A loan advertised at 9% interest can look cheaper than a loan at 9.25%. That small number feels important because it is the first thing we notice.

But here's the catch: the lowest advertised interest rate is not always the loan that costs you the least.

Processing fees, upfront deductions, a longer tenure, the way the interest rate is calculated and, in some cases, changes in a floating rate can all affect what you actually end up paying.

So instead of asking only, “Which lender has the lowest interest rate?”, ask something more useful:

“How much money will I actually get, and how much will this loan take out of my pocket before it is fully repaid?”

That is the real cost of borrowing.

What does a loan really cost?

Think about a ₹10 lakh loan.

The bank may approve ₹10 lakh, but that doesn't necessarily mean ₹10 lakh reaches your account. There could be an applicable processing fee or another disclosed charge deducted at the time of disbursement.

At the other end, you may spend several years making EMIs.

So there are really two sides to the calculation:

Money coming to you: the amount actually disbursed.

Money going from you: EMIs, interest and applicable charges over the life of the loan.

The difference between those two gives you a much better idea of what the borrowing actually costs.

The interest rate is still important. It is usually one of the biggest costs. It just isn't the whole picture.

Why does a “9% loan” not tell you enough?

Suppose you see two offers.

Loan A: 9.00%

Loan B: 9.25%

Most people will immediately lean toward Loan A.

But now imagine Loan A has a significantly higher processing fee, while Loan B has a lower fee.

If you are borrowing a large amount, that fee difference can be thousands of rupees.

Now add the tenure.

If Loan A is for a longer period, you could end up paying interest for more years even though the rate is lower.

This is why comparing loans by one number is risky.

You need to look at the whole offer.

How much interest will you actually pay?

For a standard reducing-balance EMI loan, the basic calculation is straightforward.

Total repayment = EMI × number of EMIs

Then:

Total interest = total repayment − principal borrowed

Let's say you borrow ₹10 lakh for five years and the EMI works out to approximately ₹21,247.

You make 60 payments.

That means your scheduled EMI payments are roughly ₹12.75 lakh.

You borrowed ₹10 lakh.

So approximately ₹2.75 lakh represents interest.

That's the number that tells you what the 10% rate means in actual rupees for this particular loan.

The rate is useful for comparing loans.

The total interest tells you what the rate means for your wallet.

Your EMI is not the price of the loan

This sounds obvious, but it is easy to forget when looking at loan advertisements.

Suppose someone tells you:

“Your EMI will be only ₹18,000.”

That sounds comfortable.

But ₹18,000 for how long?

Three years?

Five years?

Ten years?

Those are completely different loans.

A longer tenure can reduce the monthly EMI while increasing the total interest paid.

That is why you should never compare two loans using EMI alone.

Whenever you see an EMI, look immediately for:

  • Loan tenure

  • Total number of payments

  • Total interest

  • Total repayment

A low EMI can be helpful for your monthly budget.

It does not automatically mean the loan is cheaper.

What happens when the lender deducts the processing fee?

This is where the calculation becomes more interesting.

Suppose:

Loan approved: ₹5,00,000

Processing fee: ₹10,000

If the lender deducts the fee before disbursement, you may receive:

₹4,90,000

But your repayment obligation is still based on the loan terms for the sanctioned principal.

So you have effectively received ₹4.90 lakh while taking on repayment of a ₹5 lakh loan.

That ₹10,000 is not interest.

But it is still part of the cost of getting the loan.

Current Indian personal-loan information also highlights this exact issue: processing fees may be deducted upfront, reducing the amount the borrower actually receives.

This is one of the simplest ways to see why the advertised interest rate doesn't tell the entire story.

What other charges should you check?

The exact charges depend on the loan.

For example, a home loan may involve property valuation or legal expenses. A personal loan may have a processing fee and other applicable charges. A secured business loan can have its own documentation or valuation costs.

Depending on the product, you may come across:

  • Processing fees

  • Documentation charges

  • Legal charges

  • Property valuation or technical charges

  • Insurance-related costs where applicable

  • Statutory charges

  • Other disclosed third-party charges

  • Prepayment or foreclosure charges, where applicable

  • Penal charges for certain defaults

Don't assume all of these will apply to your loan.

That's not the point.

The point is to look at the actual charges attached to your particular offer instead of assuming the interest rate covers everything.

What is APR and why is it useful?

APR stands for Annual Percentage Rate.

In simple terms, it is intended to give you an annualized view of the cost of credit after taking relevant charges into account.

That makes it useful when two loans have different fees or other costs.

For applicable loans, the RBI's Key Facts Statement framework requires disclosure of APR and other important information so borrowers can get a clearer picture of the cost of credit.

Imagine you have:

Loan A

Loan B

Advertised interest rate

10.00%

10.25%

APR

10.70%

10.55%

If you looked only at the advertised rate, Loan A appears cheaper.

The APR gives you another piece of information that may change how you view the two offers.

But don't treat APR as a magic number either. Read what is included and check the actual KFS and loan terms.

What is the difference between interest rate and APR?

They are related, but they aren't the same thing.

Interest rate: the rate charged on the loan under its interest terms.

APR: an annualized measure intended to capture the cost of credit, including relevant charges covered by the applicable framework.

So if a lender says:

Interest rate: 10%

that doesn't necessarily mean:

Total borrowing cost: exactly 10%.

The second statement is much broader.

This is also why the RBI's KFS framework is useful. It brings important loan information into a standardized disclosure rather than leaving the borrower to piece everything together from advertisements and conversations with sales representatives.

Why does the loan tenure matter so much?

Here's a simple situation.

You need ₹20 lakh.

You can repay it over five years or ten years.

The ten-year option will generally give you a lower EMI.

That may be exactly what you need if your monthly budget is tight.

But there is a trade-off.

You are keeping the loan outstanding for much longer.

That usually means more interest over the life of the loan.

So don't look at the question as:

“Which EMI is lower?”

Look at it as:

“How much monthly payment can I comfortably handle without unnecessarily extending the loan?”

The cheapest theoretical loan isn't useful if the EMI puts too much pressure on your monthly finances.

At the same time, stretching a loan simply to make the EMI look attractive can cost considerably more over time.

What if the interest rate is floating?

This matters particularly for longer loans.

A floating interest rate can change during the loan period according to the applicable benchmark and reset mechanism.

So the EMI shown when you take the loan may not remain unchanged for the entire tenure.

For RBI-regulated floating-rate personal loans covered by its relevant framework, lenders are required to communicate the impact of interest-rate resets and provide information about changes in EMI or tenure.

Before taking a floating-rate loan, find out:

  • Which benchmark is used?

  • What is the lender's spread?

  • How often is the rate reset?

  • What happens when the rate increases?

  • Does the EMI change?

  • Can the tenure increase?

  • How will the lender tell you about the change?

You don't need to predict future interest rates.

You just need to understand what happens to your loan if the rate moves.

A small rate difference can become a big rupee difference

Suppose you borrow ₹10 lakh.

A difference of 0.25 percentage point may not look dramatic.

But if the loan runs for several years, that difference is applied across a large outstanding balance.

On a large home loan or business loan, even a small rate difference can become meaningful.

On the other hand, if one lender charges a much higher upfront fee, that can also change the comparison.

This is why there is no useful rule such as:

“Always choose the lowest rate.”

The numbers need to be calculated together.

What if the higher-rate loan has much lower fees?

Let's make the comparison practical.

Loan A

₹10 lakh

10% interest

₹25,000 processing fee

Loan B

₹10 lakh

10.25% interest

₹5,000 processing fee

Loan A saves you money through the lower interest rate.

But it starts with ₹20,000 more in fees.

The question becomes:

Does the interest saving from Loan A make up for that extra ₹20,000?

If the saving is only ₹8,000, it doesn't.

If the saving is ₹30,000, the picture is different.

This is a much more sensible comparison than simply looking at 10% versus 10.25%.

The amount you receive matters just as much as the amount you borrow

This is an especially useful point for personal loans and other loans where upfront fees can be deducted.

Suppose:

Sanctioned loan: ₹5,00,000

Upfront charges: ₹15,000

Money credited: ₹4,85,000

If you only write down “₹5 lakh loan at 10%”, you are missing something important.

You didn't actually get ₹5 lakh in your hands.

You got ₹4.85 lakh.

Yet the loan agreement is based on the sanctioned borrowing amount and its repayment terms.

That is why comparing net disbursal alongside the repayment schedule gives a more realistic view of the borrowing cost.

Don't forget about prepayment

Your original loan calculation assumes that you follow the scheduled repayment plan.

Real life doesn't always work that way.

Maybe you get a bonus.

Maybe your business has a particularly good year.

Maybe you sell an asset.

Maybe you simply decide that you want to get rid of the debt sooner.

A part-prepayment can reduce the outstanding principal.

That can reduce future interest.

So the total interest shown at the beginning of the loan isn't necessarily the amount you'll eventually pay if you make prepayments.

If you expect to prepay, check the applicable terms before choosing the loan.

And don't assume that every lender or every loan has the same prepayment rules.

Your expected time with the loan changes the calculation

This is an easy detail to miss.

Suppose two lenders charge similar interest rates.

One has a ₹20,000 upfront fee.

The other charges ₹5,000.

If you expect to keep the loan for ten years, that difference may be relatively small compared with the total interest.

But what if you expect to refinance or close the loan after one year?

Now that ₹15,000 difference matters much more.

The shorter your actual borrowing period, the more attention you should pay to upfront charges.

This is particularly relevant if you are comparing loans with the intention of transferring or prepaying them later.

What should you look for in the KFS?

For applicable loans, the Key Facts Statement is one of the documents worth reading before accepting the offer.

Don't just look at the first page and move on.

Check the important numbers.

Look for:

  • Loan amount

  • Tenure

  • Interest rate

  • Fixed or floating rate

  • APR

  • Processing fee

  • Other applicable charges

  • Repayment schedule

  • Prepayment-related terms

  • Penal charges

  • Information about changes to the interest rate, where applicable

The RBI's framework is specifically designed to provide borrowers with important loan information in a standardized form.

If someone verbally promises you a fee waiver, don't rely on the conversation alone.

Ask for it in writing.

A simple example: ₹10 lakh loan

Let's put everything together.

Suppose you borrow:

₹10,00,000

Interest rate:

10% p.a.

Tenure:

5 years

Assume the EMI is approximately:

₹21,247

Over 60 months, the scheduled repayment is approximately:

₹12.75 lakh

So the scheduled interest is around:

₹2.75 lakh

Now add a ₹15,000 processing fee.

Your cost is no longer simply the ₹2.75 lakh interest figure.

And if the fee is deducted before disbursement, you may receive only:

₹9.85 lakh

while taking on the repayment associated with the ₹10 lakh principal.

That doesn't mean the loan is automatically bad or expensive.

It means you now understand it better.

That's the whole purpose of calculating the true cost.

What about GST on loan charges?

This is one area where borrowers should avoid making assumptions.

GST treatment can depend on the particular service or charge.

For example, a lender may show a processing fee separately from applicable taxes.

So if your lender's fee is shown as:

₹10,000 + applicable tax

don't treat ₹10,000 as the final amount until you check the actual loan documents.

At the same time, don't automatically add GST to every cost you see in a generic article.

Use the amount and tax treatment stated in your actual offer.

What is the easiest way to compare two loan offers?

You don't need a complicated financial model.

Make a small table.

Offer A

Offer B

Loan amount

₹10 lakh

₹10 lakh

Interest rate

Fixed/floating

Tenure

EMI

Total interest

Processing fee

Other applicable charges

Net amount received

APR

Prepayment terms

Total scheduled repayment

Once you fill this in, the comparison becomes much clearer.

You may even discover that the loan with the slightly higher rate is cheaper overall.

Or the opposite.

The calculation decides that—not the advertisement.

Five questions worth asking before accepting the loan

Before you sign, ask the lender:

How much will actually be credited to my account?

What will I pay in processing and other charges?

What is the APR shown in my KFS?

Can the interest rate change during the loan?

What will it cost me if I repay the loan early?

These questions are simple.

They can also prevent a lot of confusion later.

Don't let the smallest number make the decision for you

A 9% interest rate looks attractive.

A ₹15,000 processing fee looks small.

A ₹20,000 EMI looks manageable.

But none of those numbers makes sense by itself.

A lower EMI could come with a much longer tenure.

A lower rate could come with higher upfront charges.

A small processing fee could sit alongside a higher interest rate.

A floating-rate loan could start at one rate and change later.

The loan needs to be viewed as one complete package.

So, what is the true cost of a loan?

In simple terms, start with the money you actually receive and compare it with everything you are expected to pay.

That includes the scheduled interest and applicable fees and charges.

For a basic comparison, look at:

Net amount received

Monthly EMI

Total interest

Total applicable charges

Total scheduled repayment

APR, where provided

Prepayment and rate-reset terms

You don't need to turn yourself into a banker.

You just need to stop comparing loans using one percentage.

The advertised interest rate is a starting point.

The real question is what the loan does to your money from the day it is disbursed until the day the balance becomes zero.

And that is the number worth comparing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the advertised interest rate the final cost of a loan?

No. The advertised interest rate is only one part of the borrowing cost. You should also check applicable processing fees, other disclosed charges, the amount actually disbursed, the loan tenure, total interest and the APR where it is provided.

Why is the total interest higher than the advertised interest rate?

The interest rate is a percentage, while total interest is the actual amount paid over the repayment period. The tenure and outstanding loan balance determine how much interest accumulates over time.

Does a processing fee increase the cost of a loan?

Yes. A processing fee is an additional borrowing cost. If it is deducted before disbursement, you receive less money while still taking the loan under the agreed repayment terms.

What is the difference between EMI and total loan cost?

EMI is the amount you pay periodically. Total loan cost looks at the full picture, including interest and applicable fees and charges over the repayment period.

What is APR on a loan?

APR, or Annual Percentage Rate, is an annualized measure intended to reflect the cost of credit after taking relevant charges into account. For applicable loans, the APR is disclosed in the Key Facts Statement.

Is a lower interest rate always a cheaper loan?

No. A loan with a lower interest rate can have higher upfront fees or other costs. Comparing the overall cost gives you a better picture than comparing the interest rate alone.

Does a longer loan tenure increase the total cost?

It can. A longer tenure usually lowers the EMI but keeps the loan outstanding for a longer period. This can result in more total interest being paid.

Can prepayment reduce the total interest on a loan?

It can. Reducing the outstanding principal earlier can reduce the interest charged in the future. The actual saving depends on the loan terms, timing and applicable prepayment conditions.

What should I check before accepting a loan offer?

Check the loan amount, actual amount disbursed, interest rate, EMI, tenure, total interest, applicable fees and charges, APR where provided, rate-reset terms for floating-rate loans, and applicable prepayment or foreclosure conditions.

Where can I find the important loan charges and terms?

For loans covered by the applicable RBI Key Facts Statement framework, the KFS is an important document to review before accepting the loan. It presents key information such as the loan terms, APR, applicable charges and repayment schedule.

posts.seoDescription: Wondering why your loan balance barely drops after years of EMIs? Learn how loan amortisation works, why early payments go mostly to interest, and how to track true debt.
posts.title: Loan Amortisation Explained: Why Your Early EMIs Barely Reduce the Principal
posts.content:
You can pay your EMI faithfully every month and still feel surprised when you check your loan statement. After a year or two of payments, the outstanding principal may have fallen much less than you expected. The reason is the way a loan is amortised.

Quick Answer: Loan amortisation is the process of gradually repaying a loan through regular payments that cover both interest and principal. In the early months, interest takes a larger share because the outstanding balance is highest. As the balance falls, more of each EMI goes toward principal.

Why Early EMIs Mostly Pay Interest Rather Than Principal

The explanation is simpler than it first appears.

With a normal reducing-balance EMI loan, you owe interest on the amount that is still outstanding. At the beginning of the loan, you owe almost the entire amount you borrowed, so the interest calculation starts from a large balance.

Your EMI then covers that month's interest, and whatever remains reduces the principal.

After that payment, your outstanding balance becomes slightly smaller. The next month's interest is calculated on that lower balance. As the balance continues to fall, the interest component gradually becomes smaller and a larger portion of the EMI can go toward principal.

RBI describes an amortisation schedule as a table showing periodic principal and interest payments along with the outstanding amount as the loan is repaid.

That changing split is the key to understanding why your loan balance can appear to fall slowly at the beginning.

What Is Loan Amortisation in Simple Words?

Think of amortisation as a repayment roadmap.

Every EMI does two jobs:

  • It pays the interest due for that period.

  • It reduces the amount you borrowed.

The exact split changes over time.

At the start:

More interest + less principal

Later:

Less interest + more principal

The EMI itself may remain almost unchanged in a fixed-rate loan, but the amount doing each job changes.

This is why looking only at your EMI doesn't tell you how quickly your actual debt is disappearing.

How Is Interest Calculated on a Reducing-Balance Loan?

Suppose you borrow ₹10 lakh at 10% per year.

For a simple monthly illustration, the monthly rate is:

10% ÷ 12 = 0.8333%

If the outstanding balance is ₹10 lakh at the beginning of the first month, the interest for that month is approximately:

₹10,00,000 × 0.8333% = ₹8,333

If your EMI is around ₹9,650, approximately ₹8,333 covers interest and roughly ₹1,317 reduces the principal.

The following month, the outstanding balance is slightly lower. The interest is therefore slightly lower too.

That leaves a little more of the EMI available for principal repayment.

The process repeats every month.

ICICI Bank similarly explains the monthly reducing-balance method as calculating interest on the remaining loan balance, with the interest component reducing as the outstanding amount comes down.

Worked Example: ₹10 Lakh Loan at 10% for 20 Years

A long tenure makes the effect particularly easy to see.

Consider this illustration:

Loan detail

Example

Loan amount

₹10,00,000

Interest rate

10% p.a.

Tenure

20 years

Number of EMIs

240

Approx. EMI

₹9,650

The first EMI is approximately ₹9,650.

Of that payment:

  • Interest: about ₹8,333

  • Principal: about ₹1,317

So only a relatively small part of the first payment reduces the amount you owe.

Now look at the first year as a whole.

Approximately:

  • Total EMI payments: ₹1.16 lakh

  • Principal repaid: ₹16,547

  • Interest paid: ₹99,255

  • Balance remaining after 12 months: about ₹9.83 lakh

This is the part that often catches borrowers off guard.

You may have paid more than ₹1 lakh during the year, but the principal has fallen by only around ₹16,500.

That doesn't mean the calculation is wrong. It is the natural result of paying interest on a balance that was close to ₹10 lakh throughout that first year.

The figures above are an illustration using a constant rate and standard monthly reducing-balance assumptions. Your lender's actual schedule can differ because of the loan agreement, disbursement date, repayment dates, rate resets, rounding and other terms.

Why Doesn't My Loan Principal Fall Quickly in the First Few Years?

The main reason is the size of the outstanding balance.

Imagine two borrowers paying the same EMI.

One owes ₹10 lakh.

The other owes ₹5 lakh.

Even if they have the same interest rate, the interest calculated on ₹10 lakh will be larger. That leaves less of the EMI available to reduce principal.

This is why the early years of a long loan can feel slow.

There is another factor: tenure.

A longer tenure generally produces a lower required EMI, but the loan remains outstanding for more years. That gives interest more time to accumulate. RBI notes that longer loan tenures can reduce the monthly EMI while increasing the overall interest burden.

So an affordable EMI doesn't automatically mean the loan is inexpensive.

Does the Bank Take Interest First?

No.

This is a common misunderstanding.

A reducing-balance loan does not normally work by taking all the interest for the first few years and only then starting to reduce the principal.

Instead, interest is calculated for each repayment period based on the outstanding balance.

Your payment covers that period's interest, and the remaining amount reduces principal.

Because the balance is highest at the beginning, the interest amount is highest at the beginning.

That's why the principal component is smaller.

As the balance falls, the interest amount falls too.

How Does the EMI Split Change Every Month?

Let's stay with the ₹10 lakh example.

The first month's interest is approximately ₹8,333.

After the first EMI, the balance is lower.

The second month's interest is therefore calculated on a slightly smaller amount.

The difference might not look impressive from one month to the next. But repeat that process for years and the effect becomes significant.

Eventually, the interest component can become much smaller than it was at the beginning, while the principal component becomes much larger.

This is why an amortisation schedule gradually changes from a loan dominated by interest payments toward one dominated by principal repayment.

Pro Tip: Want to see your own amortisation schedule? Test your numbers in our Loan Amortisation Calculator above.

What Is an Amortisation Schedule and What Does It Show?

An amortisation schedule breaks your entire repayment into individual periods.

A typical schedule may show:

Column

Meaning

Payment number

Which EMI you are looking at

Opening balance

Amount owed before that payment

EMI

Scheduled payment

Interest

Interest charged for that period

Principal

Amount reducing the loan

Closing balance

Amount still owed afterward

Some lenders provide additional information.

ICICI Bank, for example, describes repayment schedules as showing information such as tenure, outstanding duration and the interest/principal breakup of the EMI.

Once you understand these columns, your loan statement becomes much easier to follow.

Why Your Outstanding Loan Balance Matters More Than EMIs Already Paid

Borrowers often say:

"I have already paid five years of EMIs."

That's useful information, but it doesn't tell you how much debt remains.

The more important number is your outstanding principal.

You could have paid 60 EMIs and still owe a substantial amount, especially if the original loan had a long tenure.

When you're considering a prepayment, foreclosure or balance transfer, the outstanding balance is the number you need to know.

The number of EMIs you've already paid tells you how long you've been paying.

The outstanding principal tells you how much you still owe.

Those are two very different things.

How Loan Tenure Affects Principal Reduction

Loan tenure has a major effect on amortisation.

A longer tenure normally reduces the required EMI because the repayment is spread over more months.

But that also means the principal can take longer to come down.

Consider the basic trade-off:

Shorter tenure

  • Higher EMI

  • Faster principal reduction

  • Usually lower total interest

Longer tenure

  • Lower EMI

  • Slower principal reduction

  • Usually higher total interest

The right choice depends on your income, expenses and financial goals. A lower EMI can be useful if a higher payment would put too much pressure on your monthly budget.

The mistake is assuming that the lowest EMI is automatically the best loan structure.

Why Two People Paying the Same EMI Can Reduce Their Debt at Different Speeds

Suppose two borrowers both pay ₹20,000 every month.

It would be easy to assume that both are reducing their loans by roughly the same amount.

That's not necessarily true.

One borrower may have a lower interest rate.

Another may have a higher outstanding balance.

The amount of interest charged each month will therefore be different.

The borrower paying more interest has less of the ₹20,000 left over to reduce principal.

This is why the EMI by itself doesn't tell you how quickly your debt is disappearing.

What Happens to Amortisation When Interest Rates Rise or Fall?

The example above assumes that the interest rate stays unchanged.

Floating-rate loans are different.

If the applicable interest rate changes, the repayment schedule can change as well. Depending on the loan terms and lender's method, the change may affect:

  • EMI

  • Remaining tenure

  • Or both

For example, if your interest rate increases but your EMI remains unchanged, more of that EMI may initially be needed to cover interest. If the lender instead increases the EMI, your monthly payment rises.

On a long-term loan, even a relatively small rate change can have a meaningful effect on the repayment schedule.

That is why borrowers with floating-rate loans should periodically check their revised repayment details rather than relying indefinitely on the original amortisation schedule.

What Happens to the Amortisation Schedule After a Prepayment?

A prepayment reduces the outstanding principal.

That matters because future interest is calculated using the outstanding balance.

Suppose your outstanding loan is ₹40 lakh and you make a ₹5 lakh principal prepayment.

If the full amount is applied to principal, the balance could fall to roughly ₹35 lakh, subject to your lender's accounting and the terms of the loan.

The future repayment schedule then starts from a much lower balance.

Depending on the lender and the option you select, the result can be:

  • Lower EMI

  • Shorter tenure

  • Or a combination determined under the loan terms

The important point is that a prepayment is not simply "one extra EMI."

It changes the balance used for future interest calculations.

Why an Early Prepayment Can Have a Bigger Long-Term Effect

Suppose you have ₹2 lakh available for a loan prepayment.

If you reduce the principal earlier, the lower balance can affect many future interest calculations.

If you wait several years, there are fewer remaining periods in which that lower balance can make a difference.

That's why timing matters.

This doesn't mean everyone should immediately use spare cash to repay a loan. You also need to consider emergency savings, other debts, investment goals and any applicable loan terms.

But if you're considering prepayment, an amortisation schedule helps you understand the financial effect instead of guessing.

How to Check Your Loan Amortisation Schedule

You don't need to study hundreds of rows.

Start with a few important points.

Look at the:

First EMI

How much went toward interest and how much reduced principal?

End of Year 1

How much principal has actually disappeared?

End of Year 5

How much do you still owe?

Current month

What is your actual outstanding balance?

Remaining tenure

How many payments are still left?

These numbers give you a much better understanding of the loan than simply knowing your EMI.

Why Your Bank Statement and an Online EMI Calculator May Differ

An online calculator works with the assumptions you enter.

Your actual loan has its own history.

Differences can arise because of:

  • Actual disbursement date

  • Part-disbursement

  • Interest-rate resets

  • Repayment dates

  • Daily or monthly interest calculations

  • Rounding

  • Prepayments

  • Changes in EMI

  • Changes in tenure

  • Other contractual adjustments

For example, a construction-linked home loan may be disbursed in stages. In such cases, the interest situation can differ from a simple example where the entire loan amount is assumed to be disbursed on Day 1.

RBI's housing-loan FAQ notes that where a loan is disbursed in instalments, interest can be payable on the amount already disbursed before regular EMI repayment begins.

So use an online calculator to understand the mathematics and compare scenarios, but use your lender's statement and loan documents for the actual account position.

What Is Pre-EMI Interest and How Is It Different?

Pre-EMI interest can confuse borrowers because it doesn't behave exactly like a normal fully amortising EMI schedule.

It can arise when a loan is disbursed in stages, such as in some under-construction property transactions.

Instead of immediately paying a full EMI against the entire sanctioned amount, the borrower may initially pay interest on the amount that has actually been disbursed.

For example, if a lender has sanctioned ₹50 lakh but only ₹15 lakh has been disbursed, the interest calculation may initially be based on the amount disbursed rather than the entire sanctioned amount, according to the applicable loan terms.

This is one reason why the sanctioned amount, disbursed amount and outstanding amount should not be treated as the same thing.

How Amortisation Helps When Comparing Different Loan Tenures

Suppose you're deciding between two repayment periods.

The longer option may look attractive because the EMI is lower.

But don't stop there.

Compare the outstanding principal after:

  • 12 months

  • 36 months

  • 60 months

  • 120 months

Then compare the total interest paid during those periods.

This gives you a better sense of what you're buying with the lower EMI.

You're not simply choosing a payment amount.

You're choosing how quickly you want to get rid of the debt.

What Should You Look at Before Taking a Long-Term Loan?

Before signing up for a long loan, look beyond the monthly EMI.

Check:

  • Loan amount

  • Interest rate

  • Tenure

  • EMI

  • Total interest

  • Outstanding balance at different points

  • Prepayment terms

  • Rate-reset terms if applicable

  • Effect of a possible rate increase

A useful question is:

"If I continue paying this EMI, how much will I still owe after five years?"

That answer can sometimes be more revealing than the EMI itself.

Why Amortisation Is More Useful Than Just Knowing Your EMI

An EMI tells you what leaves your bank account each month.

An amortisation schedule tells you what happens to the debt.

That difference matters.

Two loans can have similar EMIs but very different repayment paths. One may reduce the principal faster, while another keeps a larger balance outstanding for longer.

Once you can read an amortisation schedule, you can also make better decisions about prepayments, tenure changes and refinancing.

You don't need to become a finance expert.

You just need to understand where each part of your EMI is going.

How to Use a Loan Amortisation Calculator

A loan amortisation calculator can make this much easier.

Enter:

  • Loan amount

  • Interest rate

  • Tenure

Then look beyond the EMI.

Check the repayment schedule and see how the balance changes month by month.

Try changing the tenure.

Then try a different interest rate.

If the calculator supports additional payments or prepayments, test those too.

For example, adding a small extra payment every month can show how much faster the principal could fall under the calculator's assumptions.

The purpose isn't to predict your lender's exact future statement.

It is to help you understand the shape of your repayment.

The Bigger Lesson: EMI Is Only One Number

When people discuss loans, the conversation often starts and ends with the EMI.

"What's the EMI?"

"Can I afford the EMI?"

"How much lower is the EMI?"

Those are useful questions, but they're only part of the story.

A loan is a moving balance.

Every month, some money pays for the cost of borrowing and some money reduces the debt itself.

Amortisation lets you see that movement.

And once you see it, several other loan decisions become easier to understand.

You can see why a longer tenure increases the interest burden.

You can see why an early prepayment can have a larger long-term effect.

You can see why a rate increase matters.

And you can see why two loans with similar EMIs may leave you with very different outstanding balances.

Final Takeaway

Early EMIs can feel frustrating because a large part of the payment may go toward interest while only a smaller amount reduces the principal.

But the reason is straightforward: interest is being calculated on a large outstanding balance.

As you repay principal, the balance becomes smaller. That reduces the interest calculation, leaving more of the EMI available to reduce principal.

The process continues until the loan is fully repaid.

If you want to understand your own loan, don't look only at the EMI.

Look at the amortisation schedule.

Check how much principal you've actually repaid, how much interest you've paid, and how much you still owe.

And if you're considering a new loan, compare the repayment path—not just the monthly payment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do early EMIs mostly pay interest?

Because the outstanding loan balance is highest at the beginning. Interest is calculated on that balance, so the interest component takes up a larger share of the EMI. As the balance falls, the interest component normally falls too.

Does my EMI reduce the principal every month?

Yes. In a standard reducing-balance EMI loan, the EMI covers the applicable interest and the remaining amount reduces the principal, subject to the terms of the loan.

Why is my outstanding balance still high after several years?

A long tenure, relatively high interest rate and the structure of the original repayment schedule can cause the principal to fall slowly during the early years.

Is a lower EMI always better?

Not necessarily. A lower EMI may come from a longer tenure, which can keep the debt outstanding for longer and increase the total interest paid.

What does an amortisation schedule show?

It normally shows each payment, the interest component, the principal component and the outstanding balance after the payment.

Does prepayment change my amortisation schedule?

Yes. A principal prepayment reduces the outstanding balance and can change the future repayment path. Depending on the loan terms, it may reduce the tenure, EMI or both.

Can a floating interest rate change my amortisation schedule?

Yes. A rate change can affect the EMI, remaining tenure or both, depending on the lender's terms and how the loan is structured.

Why is my bank's repayment schedule different from an online calculator?

Online calculators use assumptions. Your actual loan may involve different disbursement dates, rate resets, repayment dates, rounding, prepayments or other contractual details.

Should I look at my EMI or outstanding principal?

Look at both. The EMI tells you your regular payment. The outstanding principal tells you how much of the actual debt remains.

Is amortisation useful only for home loans?

No. Amortisation principles are relevant to many EMI-based reducing-balance loans, although the exact calculation and repayment terms depend on the specific loan product.
